A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpenMind dataset and SSL benchmarking project, and their text, tables, figures, and appendices are readable. The original DWI appendix is retained as Appendix B.2 in v2; the substantial expansion supports a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 2.1 and Table 1 report original descriptive results from dataset curation, including 114,570 volumes, 34,191 participants, and 23 modalities. These are dataset characterization results; v1 explicitly defers the SSL benchmark experiments.

after.justification: v2 reports original segmentation and classification experiments, fine-tuning and preprocessing ablations, hyperparameter studies, and additional dataset analyses in the main text and Appendices A–D.

M1.justification: Beyond v1's dataset construction pipeline and announced benchmark, v2 introduces operational adaptations of SSL methods to ResEnc-L and Primus-M. These include 3D SimCLR, architecture-specific dense and global output heads, and a two-layer decoder for Primus-M MAE pre-training (Figure 7 and Appendix D). These are substantial additions to the presented procedures, without establishing replacement of an earlier implemented benchmark.

E1.justification: v1 presents the pre-training corpus without downstream experiments. v2 evaluates 12 segmentation datasets and three classification datasets, covering brain and head-and-neck disease, abdominal and cardiac structures, knees, and spinal fractures across MRI and CT (Section 3.1).

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 introduce evaluated comparisons among VoCo, SwinUNETR pre-training, SimCLR, Volume Fusion, ModelsGenesis, MAE, and architecture-specific S3D or SimMIM, alongside from-scratch baselines. Table 2 also includes default nnU-Net. v1 cites several methods but reports no such comparisons.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled benchmark protocols: development versus held-out datasets, 50/50 train/test splits with additional development validation splits, common architectures, 1000-epoch pre-training, and specified fine-tuning budgets and metrics. Appendix C.2 additionally specifies five-fold classification cross-validation, although its relationship to the blanket 50/50 split statement is unclear. These protocols were absent from v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds comparisons of five fine-tuning schedules, 150 versus 1000 fine-tuning epochs, image-quality and modality filtering, and anonymization-aware reconstruction losses (Tables 4–8). Tables 10–11 add VoCo and Volume Fusion hyperparameter studies. v1 discusses possible benefits of quality scores and masks without testing them.

E5.justification: Appendix C.2 newly reports five-fold cross-validation for classification, adding resampling-based performance estimation information absent from v1. Neither version supplies seed-based variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the two-rater image-quality assessment is retained.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark and ablation results absent from v1, including mean segmentation DSC of 70.91 for ResEnc-L MAE and 70.42 for Primus-M MAE after 150 fine-tuning epochs (Table 2). Table 1 also changes OpenMind's reported volume count from 114,570 to 113,921 and modality count from 23 to 24, although some v2 prose retains 23 modalities.

T1.justification: Neither version develops theoretical guarantees, proofs, or formal assumptions. The equations and objective descriptions added in Appendix D explain established comparison methods rather than introduce substantive new mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: v1 explicitly limits its delivered contribution to the dataset and postpones benchmarking. v2 claims completed standardized benchmarking and model releases, and adds substantive conclusions about exceeding strong from-scratch baselines, task-dependent SSL effectiveness, and the competitiveness of pre-trained transformers.

C2.justification: Sections 4–5 and Appendix A add interpretations involving global versus local representations, encoder adaptation, decoder capacity, and degradation from longer fine-tuning. v2 also explicitly qualifies classification reliability, weak evidence for data-filtering benefits, and the limited pre-training budget. These empirical interpretations and limitations were absent from v1.

D1.justification: v2 replaces deferred release statements with reported availability of data, training frameworks, and model checkpoints. Appendices B–D add image-quality sampling and aggregation rules, preprocessing exceptions, optimizers, learning rates, batch sizes, augmentations, and architectural details; Section 3 specifies GPU hardware. Resource availability is reported by the PDF, not independently verified.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands its positioning around rigorous benchmarking, CNN–transformer comparisons, and data selection, adding discussion and citations for Primus, nnU-Net revisited, Touchstone, DataComp, and SemDeDup. It also adds explicit attribution to 800 source datasets through references 55–854.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and dataset narrative are extensively revised and integrated into a dataset–benchmark–results–discussion structure. The original standalone DWI appendix becomes Appendix B.2 within a reorganized four-appendix document. Authorship, affiliations, and citation presentation also change.

P2.justification: v2 introduces extensive performance and ablation tables, including color-coded result matrices, and new dataset-distribution, learning-rate, and architecture figures. Figure 1 is recomposed into a single-column montage, while the retained DWI diagram is relocated and its ADC label becomes MD. These substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v1 postpones the benchmark, leaving its intended comparative contribution unsupported. v2 supplies a controlled 15-dataset evaluation with strong baselines, targeted ablations, detailed implementation information, and explicit limitations, substantially resolving that evidentiary gap. Reporting weaknesses remain: dataset totals are inconsistent, and broad classification conclusions overlook Volume Fusion leading both Primus-M mean metrics in Table 3. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and reproducibility.
